Residues, Principal Values, and Dispersion Relations

Purdue University
Course-material provenance

This page was migrated from the CHM 696 course materials developed by Jonathan Hood and Lyudmila Slipchenko. Equations and examples remain under editorial review during the Fall 2026 website migration.

Learning goals¶

By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

  • evaluate real integrals and inverse Laplace transforms with residues;

  • define and calculate Cauchy principal values;

  • track the sign of a real-axis pole indentation; and

  • derive Kramers--Kronig relations from causality and analyticity.

Complex Numbers¶

A complex number is

z=x+iy,x,y∈R.z = x + i y, \qquad x, y \in \mathbb{R}.z=x+iy,x,y∈R.
(1)

We consider functions

f:C→C.f: \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}.f:C→C.
(2)

We can always rewrite any complex function as

f(z)=u(x,y)+i v(x,y),f(z) = u(x,y) + i\, v(x,y),f(z)=u(x,y)+iv(x,y),
(3)

where u,vu,vu,v are real-valued functions.

Complex Differentiability¶

The derivative of a complex function is

f′(z0)=lim⁡z→z0f(z)−f(z0)z−z0.f'(z_0) = \lim_{z \to z_0} \frac{f(z) - f(z_0)}{z - z_0}.f′(z0​)=z→z0​lim​z−z0​f(z)−f(z0​)​.
(4)

What the original figure plots. It shows several paths approaching the same point in the complex plane.

What this is trying to convey. Complex differentiability requires path-independent convergence of the difference quotient.

Polished version.

Key idea:

  • In R\mathbb{R}R, there is only one direction to approach.

  • In C\mathbb{C}C, there are infinitely many approach paths.

Therefore the quotient must have the same limit along every path, not merely every straight-line direction.

Holomorphic Functions¶

Note

Definition A function is holomorphic (or analytic or regular or monogenic) in a domain if it is complex differentiable at every point there.

Note

Note The statement “f(z)f(z)f(z) is analytic at a point z=az = az=a” means that f(z)f(z)f(z) has a derivative at every point inside some small circle about z=az = az=a.

Holomorphic functions are extremely well-behaved:

  • infinitely differentiable

  • equal to their Taylor series

  • integrals over closed loops vanish when the loop is contractible within the holomorphic domain

  • uniquely determined on a connected domain by values on a set with an accumulation point

Cauchy--Riemann Equations¶

Note

Theorem

If f(z)=u(x,y)+iv(x,y)f(z) = u(x,y) + iv(x,y)f(z)=u(x,y)+iv(x,y) is analytic in a region, then in that region:

ux=vy,uy=−vx.\boxed{ \begin{aligned} u_x &= v_y,\\ u_y &= -v_x. \end{aligned}}ux​uy​​=vy​,=−vx​.​​
(5)

These are the [Cauchy--Riemann (CR) conditions]{style=“color: blue”}.

Note

Theorem If CR holds, and u(x,y)u(x,y)u(x,y) and v(x,y)v(x,y)v(x,y) and their partial derivatives are continuous in a region, then f(z)f(z)f(z) is complex differentiable (holomorphic) in the region.

Complex Contour Integral¶

Complex Contour Integral¶

A contour integral ∮Cf(z)dz\oint_{C} f(z) dz∮C​f(z)dz is a line integral in the complex plane. Its value generally depends on the path CCC taken.

  • We can define the complex function f(z)f(z)f(z) and the differential dzdzdz as:

f(z)=u(x,y)+iv(x,y)dz=dx+idy\begin{aligned} f(z) &= u(x, y) + iv(x, y) \\ dz &= dx + i dy \end{aligned}f(z)dz​=u(x,y)+iv(x,y)=dx+idy​
(6)

where uuu and vvv are real functions of the real variables xxx and yyy.

  • Expanding the complex integral yields a sum of four real line integrals:

I=∮Cf(z)dz=∮Cudx−vdy⏟Real Part+i(∮Cvdx+udy)⏟Imaginary PartI = \oint_{C} f(z) dz = \underbrace{\oint_{C} u dx - v dy}_{\text{Real Part}} + i \underbrace{\left(\oint_{C} v dx + u dy\right)}_{\text{Imaginary Part}}I=∮C​f(z)dz=Real Part∮C​udx−vdy​​+iImaginary Part(∮C​vdx+udy)​​
(7)

Green’s Theorem¶

Green’s Theorem¶

Green’s theorem relates a line integral around a simple closed curve CCC to a double integral (area integral) over the enclosed region RRR bounded by CCC:

∮C(Pdx+Qdy)=∬R(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dxdy\oint_{C} (P dx + Q dy) = \iint_{R} \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right) dx dy∮C​(Pdx+Qdy)=∬R​(∂x∂Q​−∂y∂P​)dxdy
(8)

Transformation to Area Integrals via Green’s Theorem¶

Transformation to Area Integrals via Green’s Theorem¶

  • By setting P=uP=uP=u and Q=−vQ=-vQ=−v for the real part, and P=vP=vP=v and Q=uQ=uQ=u for the imaginary part, the total integral III becomes:

I=∮Cf(z)dz=∬R(∂(−v)∂x−∂u∂y)dxdy+i∬R(∂u∂x−∂v∂y)dxdy\begin{aligned} I = \oint_{C} f(z) dz = \iint_{R} \left( \frac{\partial(-v)}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} \right) dx dy + i \iint_{R} \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} \right) dx dy \end{aligned}I=∮C​f(z)dz=∬R​(∂x∂(−v)​−∂y∂u​)dxdy+i∬R​(∂x∂u​−∂y∂v​)dxdy​
(9)

  • If f(z)=u+ivf(z) = u + ivf(z)=u+iv is analytic, uuu and vvv must satisfy:

∂u∂x=∂v∂yand∂v∂x=−∂u∂y\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} = -\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}∂x∂u​=∂y∂v​and∂x∂v​=−∂y∂u​
(10)

  • This makes the integral zero:

I=0I = 0I=0
(11)

  • Thus, under the differentiability hypotheses required by Green’s theorem, the Cauchy--Riemann equations make both area integrands vanish. This proves this form of Cauchy’s theorem for a simple closed contour and its interior.

Laurent Series: Definition¶

Let f(z)f(z)f(z) be analytic on an annulus

A={z:r<∣z−z0∣<R}.A = \{ z : r < |z - z_0| < R \}.A={z:r<∣z−z0​∣<R}.
(12)

Then f(z)f(z)f(z) can be expanded in series convergent in AAA:

f(z)=∑n=−∞∞an(z−z0)n,f(z) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} a_n (z - z_0)^n,f(z)=n=−∞∑∞​an​(z−z0​)n,
(13)

where the coefficients are given by

an=12πi∮∣z−z0∣=ρf(z)(z−z0) n+1 dz,r<ρ<R.a_n = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{|z-z_0|=\rho} \frac{f(z)}{(z-z_0)^{\,n+1}}\, dz, \qquad r < \rho < R.an​=2πi1​∮∣z−z0​∣=ρ​(z−z0​)n+1f(z)​dz,r<ρ<R.
(14)

This is a [Laurent series]{style=“color: blue”}.

Structure:

  • Positive-power terms: regular (analytic) part

  • Negative-power terms: principal part

Classifying Singularities via Laurent Series¶

The Laurent series determines the nature of an isolated singularity at z0z_0z0​:

  • Removable singularity: All negative-power coefficients vanish:

a−1=a−2=⋯=0.a_{-1} = a_{-2} = \cdots = 0.a−1​=a−2​=⋯=0.
(15)

  • Pole of order mmm:

a−m≠0,but a−(m+1)=a−(m+2)=⋯=0.a_{-m} \neq 0,\quad\text{but } a_{-(m+1)} = a_{-(m+2)} = \cdots = 0.a−m​=0,but a−(m+1)​=a−(m+2)​=⋯=0.
(16)

  • Essential singularity: Infinitely many negative-power terms:

a−1,a−2,… not eventually zero.a_{-1}, a_{-2}, \dots \text{ not eventually zero}.a−1​,a−2​,… not eventually zero.
(17)

Key idea: The principal part encodes the singular behavior.

Residue of a Function at a Pole¶

If f(z)f(z)f(z) has an isolated singularity at z0z_0z0​ with Laurent expansion

f(z)=⋯+a−1z−z0+a0+a1(z−z0)+⋯ ,f(z) = \cdots + \frac{a_{-1}}{z - z_0} + a_0 + a_1 (z - z_0) + \cdots,f(z)=⋯+z−z0​a−1​​+a0​+a1​(z−z0​)+⋯,
(18)

then the residue of f(z)f(z)f(z) at z0z_0z0​ is

Res⁡(f,z0)=a−1.\operatorname{Res}(f, z_0) = a_{-1}.Res(f,z0​)=a−1​.
(19)

Interpretation: The residue is the coefficient of the (z−z0)−1(z - z_0)^{-1}(z−z0​)−1 term in the Laurent series.

Residue Theorem¶

Let f(z)f(z)f(z) be analytic in a domain except for isolated singularities z1,…,znz_1,\dots,z_nz1​,…,zn​ inside a positively oriented contour Γ\GammaΓ.

Then the [Residue Theorem]{style=“color: blue”} is valid:

∮Γf(z) dz=2πi∑k=1nRes⁡(f,zk).\oint_{\Gamma} f(z)\, dz = 2\pi i \sum_{k=1}^{n} \operatorname{Res}(f, z_k).∮Γ​f(z)dz=2πik=1∑n​Res(f,zk​).
(20)

Consequences:

  • Integral depends only on the residues inside Γ\GammaΓ.

  • Contour shape does not matter (homotopy invariance).

  • Reduces contour integrals to local expansions at singularities.

Computing Residues¶

If f(z)f(z)f(z) has a simple pole at z=z0z=z_0z=z0​, then

Res⁡z=z0f(z)=lim⁡z→z0(z−z0)f(z).\operatorname{Res}_{z=z_0} f(z) = \lim_{z\to z_0} (z - z_0) f(z).Resz=z0​​f(z)=z→z0​lim​(z−z0​)f(z).
(21)

If f(z)f(z)f(z) has a pole of order mmm at z0z_0z0​, then

Res⁡z=z0f(z)=1(m−1)!lim⁡z→z0d m−1dz m−1[(z−z0)mf(z)].\operatorname{Res}_{z=z_0}f(z) = \frac{1}{(m-1)!} \lim_{z\to z_0} \frac{d^{\,m-1}}{dz^{\,m-1}} \left[(z - z_0)^m f(z)\right].Resz=z0​​f(z)=(m−1)!1​z→z0​lim​dzm−1dm−1​[(z−z0​)mf(z)].
(22)

Special case: Pole of order 2

Res⁡z=z0f(z)=lim⁡z→z0ddz[(z−z0)2f(z)].\operatorname{Res}_{z=z_0}f(z) = \lim_{z\to z_0} \frac{d}{dz}\left[(z - z_0)^2 f(z)\right].Resz=z0​​f(z)=z→z0​lim​dzd​[(z−z0​)2f(z)].
(23)

Using Residues to Evaluate Real Integrals¶

Goal: Compute integrals of the form

∫−∞∞g(x) dx.\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x)\,dx.∫−∞∞​g(x)dx.
(24)

Method:

  1. Extend g(x)g(x)g(x) to a complex function f(z)f(z)f(z).

  2. Integrate f(z)f(z)f(z) around a contour that contains the real axis.

  3. Use Cauchy’s Residue Theorem:

∮f(z) dz=2πi∑Res⁡f(z).\oint f(z)\,dz = 2\pi i \sum \operatorname{Res} f(z).∮f(z)dz=2πi∑Resf(z).
(25)

  1. Show the integral on the large semicircle vanishes.

  2. If the contour is positively oriented, its arc contribution vanishes, and it contains no pole on the real axis, conclude

∫−∞∞g(x) dx=2πi∑Res⁡f(z).\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x)\,dx = 2\pi i\sum \operatorname{Res} f(z).∫−∞∞​g(x)dx=2πi∑Resf(z).
(26)

Example: A Standard Residue Calculation¶

Evaluate:

I=∫−∞∞dxx2+1.I = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{dx}{x^2 + 1}.I=∫−∞∞​x2+1dx​.
(27)

Complex extension:

f(z)=1z2+1=1(z−i)(z+i).f(z) = \frac{1}{z^2 + 1} = \frac{1}{(z-i)(z+i)}.f(z)=z2+11​=(z−i)(z+i)1​.
(28)

Pole inside upper semicircle: z=iz=iz=i.

Res⁡z=if(z)=lim⁡z→i(z−i)1(z−i)(z+i)=12i.\operatorname{Res}_{z=i} f(z) = \lim_{z\to i} (z-i) \frac{1}{(z-i)(z+i)} = \frac{1}{2i}.Resz=i​f(z)=z→ilim​(z−i)(z−i)(z+i)1​=2i1​.
(29)

Thus the contour integral equals:

2πi⋅12i=π.2\pi i \cdot \frac{1}{2i} = \pi.2πi⋅2i1​=π.
(30)

Semicircle contribution →0\to 0→0, so:

∫−∞∞dxx2+1=π.\boxed{ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{dx}{x^2+1} = \pi }.∫−∞∞​x2+1dx​=π​.
(31)

Semicircle Contribution Vanishes¶

Parameterize semicircle: z=Reiθ,θ∈[0,π]z = R e^{i\theta}, \theta \in [0, \pi]z=Reiθ,θ∈[0,π], dz=iReiθdθdz = i R e^{i\theta} d\thetadz=iReiθdθ.

∫semicircledzz2+1=∫0πiReiθdθR2e2iθ+1\int_{\text{semicircle}} \frac{dz}{z^2 + 1} = \int_0^\pi \frac{i R e^{i\theta} d\theta}{R^2 e^{2i\theta} + 1}∫semicircle​z2+1dz​=∫0π​R2e2iθ+1iReiθdθ​
(32)

Estimate magnitude:

∣∫semicircledzz2+1∣≤∫0πR dθR2−1=πRR2−1⟶0.\left| \int_{\text{semicircle}} \frac{dz}{z^2 + 1} \right| \leq\int_0^\pi\frac{R\,d\theta}{R^2-1} =\frac{\pi R}{R^2-1}\longrightarrow0.∣∣​∫semicircle​z2+1dz​∣∣​≤∫0π​R2−1Rdθ​=R2−1πR​⟶0.
(33)

Conclusion: Semicircle does not contribute in the limit R→∞R \to \inftyR→∞.

Real-Line Integral vs Semicircle Contribution¶

Consider the integral

∫−∞∞dxx2+1\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{dx}{x^2 + 1}∫−∞∞​x2+1dx​
(34)

computed using a semicircular contour in the upper half-plane.

Contour:

  • Real axis: −R→R-R \to R−R→R (horizontal)

  • Semicircle of radius RRR in the upper half-plane

Decomposition:

∮Cdzz2+1=∫−RRdxx2+1⏟Real-line integral (non-zero)+∫semicircledzz2+1⏟Semicircle integral (vanishes as R→∞)\oint_C \frac{dz}{z^2 + 1} = \underbrace{\int_{-R}^{R} \frac{dx}{x^2+1}}_{\text{Real-line integral (non-zero)}} + \underbrace{\int_{\text{semicircle}} \frac{dz}{z^2 + 1}}_{\text{Semicircle integral (vanishes as $R\to\infty$)}}∮C​z2+1dz​=Real-line integral (non-zero)∫−RR​x2+1dx​​​+Semicircle integral (vanishes as R→∞)∫semicircle​z2+1dz​​​
(35)

Real-Line Integral vs Semicircle Contribution - cont¶

Key points:

  • The integrand along the real axis is positive and decays as 1/x21/x^21/x2 for large ∣x∣|x|∣x∣, so the integral is finite and non-zero.

  • The semicircle integral vanishes in the limit R→∞R\to\inftyR→∞ because ∣f(z)∣∼1/R2|f(z)| \sim 1/R^2∣f(z)∣∼1/R2 for large ∣z∣|z|∣z∣.

  • Using the Residue Theorem:

∫−∞∞dxx2+1=2πi⋅Res⁡(1z2+1,i)=π\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{dx}{x^2+1} = 2\pi i \cdot \operatorname{Res}\left(\frac{1}{z^2+1}, i\right) = \pi∫−∞∞​x2+1dx​=2πi⋅Res(z2+11​,i)=π
(36)

Conclusion: Only the real-line integral contributes to the final value; the semicircle “disappears.”

Example: Evaluate a Contour Integral Using Residues¶

∮Γzz2+1 dz\oint_{\Gamma} \frac{z}{z^2 + 1} \, dz∮Γ​z2+1z​dz

where Γ\GammaΓ encloses z=iz=iz=i and z=−iz=-iz=−i.

∮Γzz2+1dz=2πi(12+12)=2πi.\oint_{\Gamma} \frac{z}{z^2+1}dz = 2\pi i \left(\frac12 + \frac12\right) = 2\pi i.∮Γ​z2+1z​dz=2πi(21​+21​)=2πi.

Example: $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}¶

\frac{\cos x}{1+x^2},dx$

Solve Integral: ∫−∞∞cos⁡x1+x2dx\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{\cos x}{1+x^2} dx∫−∞∞​1+x2cosx​dx We use the function:

The residue is

Res⁡(f,i)=lim⁡z→i(z−i)eiz(z+i)(z−i)=eii2i=e−12i.\operatorname{Res}(f,i) = \lim_{z\to i} (z-i) \frac{e^{iz}}{(z+i)(z-i)} = \frac{e^{i i}}{2i} = \frac{e^{-1}}{2i}.Res(f,i)=z→ilim​(z−i)(z+i)(z−i)eiz​=2ieii​=2ie−1​.

Inverse Laplace transform¶

Recall Laplace transform:

L{f(t)}=∫0∞f(t)e−st dt=F(s)\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = \int_0^\infty f(t) e^{-st} \, dt = F(s)L{f(t)}=∫0∞​f(t)e−stdt=F(s)
(52)

The inverse Laplace transform can be computed using [Bromwich integral]{style=“color: blue”}:

f(t)=12πi∫γ−i∞γ+i∞F(s)estds,f(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_{\gamma - i\infty}^{\gamma + i\infty} F(s)e^{st} ds,f(t)=2πi1​∫γ−i∞γ+i∞​F(s)estds,
(53)

where:

  • F(s)F(s)F(s) is the Laplace transform of f(t)f(t)f(t).

  • γ\gammaγ is chosen so that the vertical line Re(s)=γ\mathrm{Re}(s)=\gammaRe(s)=γ lies to the right of all singularities of F(s)F(s)F(s).

  • The contour can be closed and evaluated using residues.

Example¶

  • Evaluate the inverse Laplace transform for

F(s)=1s(s+1)F(s)=\dfrac{1}{s(s+1)}F(s)=s(s+1)1​
(54)

  • Poles: s=0s=0s=0 and s=−1s=-1s=−1 (both have Re⁡(s)<γ\operatorname{Re}(s)<\gammaRe(s)<γ if γ>0\gamma>0γ>0).

  • We take the Bromwich line at Re⁡(s)=γ\operatorname{Re}(s)=\gammaRe(s)=γ with γ>0\gamma>0γ>0 and close left for t>0t>0t>0 so that both poles are enclosed by the left semicircle.

  • By the residue theorem,

f(t)=∑poles insideRes⁡(F(s)est,sk).f(t)=\sum_{\text{poles inside}} \operatorname{Res}\big(F(s)e^{st},s_k\big).f(t)=poles inside∑​Res(F(s)est,sk​).
(55)

Example (continued)¶

Compute residues of F(s)est=ests(s+1)F(s)e^{st}=\dfrac{e^{st}}{s(s+1)}F(s)est=s(s+1)est​.

At s=0s=0s=0 (simple pole):

Res⁡s=0=lim⁡s→0sests(s+1)=lim⁡s→0ests+1=1.\operatorname{Res}_{s=0} = \lim_{s\to0} s\frac{e^{st}}{s(s+1)} = \lim_{s\to0}\frac{e^{st}}{s+1} = 1 .Ress=0​=s→0lim​ss(s+1)est​=s→0lim​s+1est​=1.
(56)

At s=−1s=-1s=−1 (simple pole):

Res⁡s=−1=lim⁡s→−1(s+1)ests(s+1)=lim⁡s→−1ests=−e−t.\operatorname{Res}_{s=-1} = \lim_{s\to-1}(s+1)\frac{e^{st}}{s(s+1)} = \lim_{s\to-1}\frac{e^{st}}{s} = -e^{-t}.Ress=−1​=s→−1lim​(s+1)s(s+1)est​=s→−1lim​sest​=−e−t.
(57)

Therefore

f(t)=2πi ⁣∑Res×12πi=1−e−t.f(t) = 2\pi i\!\sum\text{Res}\times\frac{1}{2\pi i} = 1 - e^{-t}.f(t)=2πi∑Res×2πi1​=1−e−t.
(58)

Cauchy Principal Value¶

Many integrals in physics and engineering contain singularities on the real axis. Examples:

∫−∞∞f(x)x−x0 dx,∫0∞sin⁡xx dx.\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{f(x)}{x-x_0} \, dx, \qquad \int_0^{\infty} \frac{\sin x}{x} \, dx.∫−∞∞​x−x0​f(x)​dx,∫0∞​xsinx​dx.
(59)

These are not defined in the usual sense. The [Cauchy Principal Value (P.V.)]{style=“color: blue”} provides a consistent interpretation.

Dispersion relations arise when such integrals appear in Fourier- or Laplace-transform problems with causality.

Cauchy Principal Value (continued)¶

For a function with a simple pole at x=ax=ax=a, the [principal value]{style=“color: blue”} integral is defined as:

P.V.∫−∞∞f(x) dx=lim⁡ϵ→0(∫−∞a−ϵf(x)dx+∫a+ϵ∞f(x)dx).\mathrm{P.V.} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, dx = \lim_{\epsilon \to 0} \left( \int_{-\infty}^{a-\epsilon} f(x) dx + \int_{a+\epsilon}^{\infty} f(x) dx \right).P.V.∫−∞∞​f(x)dx=ϵ→0lim​(∫−∞a−ϵ​f(x)dx+∫a+ϵ∞​f(x)dx).
(60)

Key idea:

  • Remove symmetric neighborhoods around the singularity.

  • Evaluate the limit as the neighborhood shrinks.

  • Works naturally with contour integration (small semicircles around pole).

Example

Consider ∫05dxx−3\int_0^5 \frac{dx}{x-3}∫05​x−3dx​.
Its principal value P.V.∫05dxx−3=ln⁡23P.V.\int_0^5 \frac{dx}{x-3} = \ln \frac{2}{3}P.V.∫05​x−3dx​=ln32​

Poles on the real axis¶

When evaluating real integrals using contour integration, poles may lie directly on the real axis (the contour of integration).

To define the integral consistently, we indent the contour with a small semicircle of radius ε\varepsilonε around the pole.

This indentation contributes a definite amount depending on whether the semicircle goes above or below the pole.

Local Behavior Near the Pole¶

Suppose f(z)f(z)f(z) has a simple pole at z=az=az=a:

f(z)∼Res⁡(f,a)z−a.f(z) \sim \frac{\operatorname{Res}(f,a)}{z-a}.f(z)∼z−aRes(f,a)​.
(61)

Parameterize the indentation:

z=a+εeiθ.z = a + \varepsilon e^{i\theta}.z=a+εeiθ.
(62)

Then

dz=iεeiθdθ.dz = i\varepsilon e^{i\theta} d\theta.dz=iεeiθdθ.
(63)

Substitute:

∫Cεf(z)dz≈∫Res⁡(f,a)εeiθiεeiθdθ=i Res⁡(f,a)∫dθ.\int_{C_\varepsilon} f(z)dz \approx \int \frac{\operatorname{Res}(f,a)}{\varepsilon e^{i\theta}} i\varepsilon e^{i\theta} d\theta = i\,\operatorname{Res}(f,a) \int d\theta.∫Cε​​f(z)dz≈∫εeiθRes(f,a)​iεeiθdθ=iRes(f,a)∫dθ.
(64)

Principal Value From Contours¶

Consider the integral

∫−∞∞f(x)x−adx,\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{f(x)}{x-a} dx,∫−∞∞​x−af(x)​dx,
(65)

in which f(z)f(z)f(z) is analytic for y≥0y\ge 0y≥0 and →0\rightarrow 0→0 at ∞\infty∞; aaa is real.

Then we can write a contour identity:

0=∮Cf(z)z−adz=if(a)∫π0dθ+P.V.∫−∞∞f(x)x−a dx,0 = \oint_C \frac{f(z)}{z-a} dz = i f(a)\int_{\pi}^{0}d\theta +\mathrm{P.V.}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{f(x)}{x-a}\,dx,0=∮C​z−af(z)​dz=if(a)∫π0​dθ+P.V.∫−∞∞​x−af(x)​dx,
(66)

for the contour that avoids the pole with a small semicircle.

Thus,

P.V.∫−∞∞f(x)x−adx=iπf(a)\mathrm{P.V.}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{f(x)}{x-a} dx = i \pi f(a)P.V.∫−∞∞​x−af(x)​dx=iπf(a)
(67)

Dispersion Relations¶

In physics, especially optics and quantum scattering, a response function F(ω)F(\omega)F(ω) often satisfies:

  • analyticity in upper half-plane,

  • decay at ∣ω∣→∞|\omega|\to\infty∣ω∣→∞,

  • real and imaginary parts are related by causality.

These conditions imply [Kramers--Kronig dispersion relations]{style=“color: blue”}.

Dispersion Relations (continued)¶

Consider a complex response function:

F(ω)=FR(ω)+iFI(ω),F(\omega) = F_R(\omega) + i F_I(\omega),F(ω)=FR​(ω)+iFI​(ω),
(68)

analytic in the upper half-plane.

For a simple contour that avoids a pole on the real axis:

∮F(z)z−ωdz=0.\oint \frac{F(z)}{z-\omega} dz = 0.∮z−ωF(z)​dz=0.
(69)

We have:

P.V.∫−∞∞F(ω′)ω′−ω dω′=iπF(ω).\mathrm{P.V.}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{F(\omega')}{\omega'-\omega}\,d\omega' =i\pi F(\omega).P.V.∫−∞∞​ω′−ωF(ω′)​dω′=iπF(ω).
(70)

Splitting real and imaginary parts gives [Kramers--Kronig relations]{style=“color: blue”}:

P.V.∫−∞∞FR(ω′)ω′−ωdω′=−πFI(ω)\mathrm{P.V.}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{F_R(\omega')}{\omega' - \omega} d\omega' = - \pi F_I(\omega)P.V.∫−∞∞​ω′−ωFR​(ω′)​dω′=−πFI​(ω)
(71)
P.V.∫−∞∞FI(ω′)ω′−ωdω′=πFR(ω)\mathrm{P.V.}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{F_I(\omega')}{\omega' - \omega} d\omega' = \pi F_R(\omega)P.V.∫−∞∞​ω′−ωFI​(ω′)​dω′=πFR​(ω)
(72)

Kramers--Kronig (KK) relations for mechanical systems¶

Mechanical oscillators (pendulum, mass--spring systems) respond to external forces with:

  • an in-phase component (elastic response),

  • an out-of-phase component (dissipative response).

These responses are encoded in the complex susceptibility

χ(ω)=χ′(ω)+iχ′′(ω).\chi(\omega) = \chi'(\omega) + i\chi''(\omega).χ(ω)=χ′(ω)+iχ′′(ω).
(73)

Because the physical system is causal, the real and imaginary parts are related by Kramers--Kronig (KK) relations.

Equation of Motion¶

Consider a damped driven mechanical oscillator:

mx¨+bx˙+kx=F0e−iωt.m\ddot{x} + b\dot{x} + kx = F_0 e^{-i\omega t}.mx¨+bx˙+kx=F0​e−iωt.
(74)

The steady-state solution is

x(ω)=χ(ω)F0,x(\omega) = \chi(\omega) F_0,x(ω)=χ(ω)F0​,
(75)

where the susceptibility is

χ(ω)=1k−mω2−ibω.\chi(\omega) = \frac{1}{k - m\omega^2 - i b\omega}.χ(ω)=k−mω2−ibω1​.
(76)

This is a causal response function ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ KK relations apply.

Real and Imaginary Parts¶

Write

χ(ω)=k−mω2(k−mω2)2+(bω)2  +  ibω(k−mω2)2+(bω)2.\chi(\omega) = \frac{k - m\omega^2}{(k - m\omega^2)^2 + (b\omega)^2} \; +\; i \frac{b\omega}{(k - m\omega^2)^2 + (b\omega)^2}.χ(ω)=(k−mω2)2+(bω)2k−mω2​+i(k−mω2)2+(bω)2bω​.
(77)
χ′(ω)=k−mω2(k−mω2)2+(bω)2\chi'(\omega) = \frac{k - m\omega^2}{(k - m\omega^2)^2 + (b\omega)^2}χ′(ω)=(k−mω2)2+(bω)2k−mω2​
(78)

controls elastic stiffness,

χ′′(ω)=bω(k−mω2)2+(bω)2\chi''(\omega) = \frac{b\omega}{(k - m\omega^2)^2 + (b\omega)^2}χ′′(ω)=(k−mω2)2+(bω)2bω​
(79)

measures dissipation.

The KK relations guarantee that loss determines stiffness and vice versa.

KK Relations¶

For any causal susceptibility:

χ′(ω)=1π P∫−∞∞χ′′(ω′)ω′−ω dω′,χ′′(ω)=−1π P∫−∞∞χ′(ω′)ω′−ω dω′.\begin{aligned} \chi'(\omega) &= \frac{1}{\pi} \, \mathrm{P} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{\chi''(\omega')}{\omega' - \omega} \, d\omega', \\ \chi''(\omega) &= -\frac{1}{\pi} \, \mathrm{P} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{\chi'(\omega')}{\omega' - \omega} \, d\omega'. \end{aligned}χ′(ω)χ′′(ω)​=π1​P∫−∞∞​ω′−ωχ′′(ω′)​dω′,=−π1​P∫−∞∞​ω′−ωχ′(ω′)​dω′.​
(80)

  • Knowing either the dissipative or elastic part determines the other.

  • Changing bbb changes both the height and width of the loss peak; χ′′\chi''χ′′ is not necessarily monotone in bbb at every fixed frequency.

  • KK relation implies a required change in the elastic response χ′\chi'χ′.

  • For a fixed causal response function, its dispersive and absorptive parts cannot be specified independently; they are Hilbert-transform pairs.

This is the mechanical analog of dispersion in optics.
